delta.statement: In-span, exactly two statements changed: `return i2v_ainfo_err(ret, tret);` became `return unsafe { i2v_ainfo_err(ret, tret) };` (line 351) and likewise at the `OPENSSL_sk_push` failure (line 376), each with a SAFETY comment. `unsafe { f(x) }` and `f(x)` compile to the same call, so no value, branch, allocation, release order or failure result moved. The helper's body (a guarded `OPENSSL_sk_pop_free` that runs only when `ret` is NULL), its destructor thunk and its private non-`#[no_mangle]` linkage are unchanged, so no symbol, ABI or observable behaviour changes; the only semantic effect is that a safe caller can no longer invoke the helper with an unchecked stack.

answers.a_safe_rust_can_cause_ub: No. The operation is a private `unsafe extern "C" fn` reached only through the row's `i2v` slot, and the helper it calls is now an `unsafe fn` with a `# Safety` contract, so no safe Rust caller can reach either with an unchecked pointer. Before b82 the helper was a safe `fn` taking two raw stacks and calling `OPENSSL_sk_pop_free` on one of them: a safe caller could have passed a non-exclusively-owned or already-released list, so this change removes a safe interface that could cause UB rather than adding unsafe surface.
answers.b_all_unsafe_covered: Yes. Inside the span every unsafe act is either an `raise_site`/constant-site call already covered by its own SAFETY comment or one of the two new `unsafe { i2v_ainfo_err(..) }` calls, each with a SAFETY comment that names the witness: `ret` is this frame's own argument and is read only for NULL; `tret` is either the caller-supplied list or the list an earlier `i2v_GENERAL_NAME` returned, every element planted by this frame and handed to nobody else, so the pop-free is its single release. The helper's `# Safety` states the same obligation for any future caller.
answers.c_hidden_obligation: None new. The obligation was always there and was hidden by a safe signature; it is now stated in the helper's `# Safety` and discharged at both call sites. The helper remains private and non-exported, so there is no new ABI, layout or symbol obligation, and no new caller appears.
answers.d_load_bearing_control: The three qualifier controls are load-bearing in the only way stable Rust admits: removing the `unsafe` qualifier makes each control fail. C1: on the candidate, `cargo test --lib -- unsafe_fn` gives 15 passed including `the_i2v_err_helper_is_an_unsafe_fn`. C2: on a test-only git-archive copy of fed1f077b with the three qualifiers removed, the same filter gives 12 passed and exactly those 3 failed (`missing unsafe fn i2v_ainfo_err(` etc.). A type-level assertion is not expressible on stable Rust and no runtime instrument can distinguish a safe-signature helper with identical codegen, which is why the control is a source-text pin; that limit is stated, not hidden.

answers.b_all_unsafe_covered: Yes. The helper's `# Safety` states the same contract for future callers, including that the pointer is non-NULL and consumed exactly once.
answers.c_hidden_obligation: None new. The obligation (exclusive ownership, single release, non-NULL) existed before and was hidden by the safe signature; it is now stated and discharged at all five exits. Private linkage means no ABI, layout or symbol obligation is added.

The qualifier controls are source-text pins. They can detect a removed `unsafe` qualifier, not a semantically equivalent re-introduction of the same obligation behind a different safe signature; that class still depends on review, not on an instrument.

The closure tool's span hash covers the operation text and attributes only; the `do_ext_nconf` dispatcher, the row tables and the registry hold remain governed by the mechanism-scope rules, not by this hash.

The mutant arm proves the controls fire; it does not prove that the safe-signature helper was ever called with a violating pointer in production (no such call was found, and the obligation was latent, not observed).
does_not_prove: That either builder is SAFE-COMPATIBLE for the consumer family; the closure verdict remains ACCEPTED with safe_compatible=false.
That no other X509 helper still hides a raw-pointer obligation behind a safe signature; this review covers exactly the three helpers fed1f077b elevated.
That the prior verdicts were wrong; they were content-bound to bytes that no longer exist at b82, which is a binding failure, not a safety regression.
